Hey [@Thom Ivy](/edgeware/account/jKauGVPCQkteGTDKuuNwhYhMBrj5QuytgybEC4A5cS4Bki5) thanks for sharing.

Few questions:

> The process of upgrading to Wako however, has revealed a deep need for technical ownership and leadership beyond what the Agency is currently able to provide.  

Can you elaborate on these issues a little more? Would help with understanding the type of skills required and aid others who may have experience in that area. 

Following that, just adding in one other paragraph that is quoted in the Polkadot wiki and is useful when considering this proposal. 

> The Technical Committee is composed of the teams that have successfully implemented or specified either a Polkadot/Kusama runtime or Polkadot Host. 

So right now what teams / individuals have achieved this in Edgeware? 

- Commonwealth Labs 
- Anyone else?


Clearly we need more competent technical folks who can level us up here - would you not say that this should be a pre-requirement? 

You make the case:

> I propose that Technical Council(TC) members in EDG are voted via Referendum, instead of Council. 

Can you just elaborate on why this would be done by referendum over council?

We have a mix of technical and DAO based skills in the council currently, so there are some who can fulfil the safety net of ensuring upgrades are done correctly. 

Not for or against, but it would be good to hear your rationale on this specific point. 

> Additionally, I believe that we should have clear commitment and requirements from candidates for Technical Committee, namely that the account belongs represents a team with significant stake-in-the-game on EDG's future. 

This makes sense, but who are the examples of this outside of CW Labs? 

> This might be a technical team with an undeployed product and EDG to bond instead as their stake, or a team with an active or deployed project. This will be a topic for later discussion. 

This returns to the earlier point about teams who have successfully deployed a new runtime to the chsin being those who should be considered for candidacy for the technical committee. 

To reiterate, are there any other teams that have deployed runtimes to EDG and have a large stake of EDG?

Returning to the key part of your argument:

> This post argues that we can more effectively describe and manage our ecosystem through a more clear division in our chain-dao concept by focusing on the two aspects individually, analyzing our efforts, governance, and labor separately. 

This is a great jumping off point for discussion - and really gets to the heart of what Edgeware is and is trying to do and should be where people really spend time to consider. 

- Is it a smart contract blockchain? (yes)
- It a layer 1 chain DAO?  (yes)
- Is it both? (yes)
- Which takes precedence? 
- In which context? 


This is s really meaty subject and is absolutely fundamental to the future of the project. 

My own view which relates back to this point is that you cannot separate the two and that an ideal scenario is collaboration and connection between layers of the project. 

So for example - with the New-Futures proposal, there is a DAO funded project that has been debated and refined over a long period and that also involves a runtime upgrade of the RMRK pallets to Edgeware.

> N-F will also aim to be one of the first projects to leverage RMRK 2.0, a Substrate standard that is currently limited to utilising Substrate’s remark functionality (graffitiing the chain), before adopting the RMRK pallets which will be included in Kabocha’s - our Kusama parachain candidate) - initial runtime deployment and **we would aim to upgrade Edgeware to accommodate.** This would lead into compatibility with WASM/Ink smart contracts as we develop additional functionality and offer composability of our New-Futures projects. 

The process is yet to be finalised, but I'm assuming [@Ramsey](/edgeware/account/k44nJ5yAhFz3XHGeTPuKvegJ4GD1YCSVaPc7wj4miVL6epN) would propose and instantiate the upgrade w/ help from [@Bruno](/edgeware/account/hm3AHvCvkdcdznNCYbGANPY3QaDZErAGb5mdFUxjXrtzZNf). 

So in this example, would [@Ramsey](/edgeware/account/k44nJ5yAhFz3XHGeTPuKvegJ4GD1YCSVaPc7wj4miVL6epN) be added to the technical committee?

He has a few million EDG and perhaps more as we put forward the Kabocha proposals - does this constitute **"a significant stake-in-the-game on EDG's future**"? 

What amount would that be and how do we decide? 

If we look at EDG as a stack, here's what we have: 

![](https://commonwealth-uploads.s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/dc5bcb4f-7964-4000-ab29-251d2da7baf4.1631868058947)

You cannot separate the utility of EDG, all EDG holders have the ability to:

1. Stake
2. Vote
3. Spend (by virtue of approving treasury spends)


The suggestion of the Technical committee being voted in by referendum is fine, but if that is to align with our stated intention to be community led, then those teams need to also have their projects funded via a referendum vote. 

To make the point another way, if a team purchased 25M EDG and wanted to deploy an app (any app) to the chain that required some new runtime, then would there be a path to them becoming a technical committee member? 

My nervousness on this point is this circumvents the elegant design of Substrate as a layer 1 chain DAO that will work best if all aspects of its core design are worked in sync, not separated and seen as unrelated elements. 

Maybe I misunderstand some of this but key question: 

Can we also add the requirement for those technical members looking to deploy to have a proposal for their project also funded by the community - e.g. their specific runtime upgrade?

Just a following note since read [@remz](/edgeware/account/kWgq9PZzqF6jYKSnZXd2tP8AiKEmm1NcQNWiwCXgfNFsWA1) post - the use of "builders" as a catchall is confusing.

This (Edgeware) is a coordination game between very different groups who all contribute value... the art is to translate between them all and not stick one particular group in some special category.

For what it's worth, I consider builders to be anyone who submits a proposal and is funded by the chain.

If we are to have a technical committee, then it should be made up of talented builders who are funded by the DAO and successfully deploy a runtime.

For the sake of transparency and adequate information regarding proposals, in all communications, let us first stop this use of purposely ambiguous terms such as "builders". 
This vocable mixes together many concepts, that people who are not tech savvy get confused with.
Below, some examples of such concepts, but not limited to:
1/ Apps developers that use the chain. Those are clients of the chain services, and the chain ought to wait for some kind of value transfer as a payment. 
2/ Consultants who are providing incremental updates on the chain, following for examples substrate upgrades. The chain is client of those.
3/ People who develop websites, chat programs, conferencing software etc. that are used in one way or another by the chain. The chain may be client of those programs, or chose to fund some or not, depending on what it wants to use.
4/ Talented developers that can build a blockchain from scratch and with a vision. Those are for example, the core contributors of substrate.

As mentioned, there could be many other categories, but mixing them is maintaining an unhealthy confusion. 
For example, the proposal for partnership you are referring to was amounting to paying people that ought to be client of the chain, without ensuring any value transfer in return. A partner is not the idea of an app that is "Well funded" by a VC, and for which Edgeware would pay the VC back with a significant portion of the chain to potentially deploy there (and probably everywhere else anyway). This vocable mixes together many concepts, that people who are not tech savvy get confused with.

1/ Apps developers that use the chain. Those are clients of the chain services, and the chain ought to wait for some kind of value transfer as a payment. 
2/ Consultants who are providing incremental updates on the chain, following for examples substrate upgrades. The chain is client of those.
3/ People who develop websites, chat programs, conferencing software etc. that are used in one way or another by the chain. The chain may be client of those programs, or chose to fund some or not, depending on what it wants to use.
4/ Talented developers that can build a blockchain from scratch and with a vision. Those are for example, the core contributors of substrate.

As mentioned, there could be many other categories, but mixing them is maintaining an unhealthy confusion. 
For example, the proposal for partnership you are referring to was amounting to paying people that ought to be client of the chain, without ensuring any value transfer in return. A partner is not the idea of an app that is "Well funded" by a VC, and for which Edgeware would pay the VC back with a significant portion of the chain to potentially deploy there (and probably everywhere else anyway). A partner could be a VC investing directly in the chain for instance.
Or it could be an app where the value transfer would be greater or equal than the funding provided etc. 

Now about the technical council in particular.

> The process of upgrading to Wako however, has revealed a deep need for technical ownership and leadership beyond what the Agency is currently able to provide.

Could you elaborate on that point? So far, upgrades have been proposed through a standard democracy proposals. The agency had no need to conduct those upgrades itself, and I am not sure about what changed. We can perfectly have people consulting for the chain for incremental upgrades without "taking ownership"

Now assuming a technical council would be relevant, category 4 is what ought to be in such an entity. 
**Issue 1: **We have currently nobody from category 4 who would qualify as a potential member of such a committee.
**Issue 2:** Fast tracking is possible through the council. It has been performed once already for a runtime bugfix. There is no other reason to conduct fast-tracking. I am not aware of any lost opportunity so far due to upgrades being centralised within a small set of happy fews within 3 days rather than through a proper vote within 7 days.
**Issue 3:** The regular council has been abuse to misappropriate funds in the past. The technical council, through its ability to push for updates without other control has arguably a greater power. I am generally totally against creating additional centralisation entities, unless there is a clear positive purpose. 
I see no such argument supporting this in the above writing.
